analysis.one_liner: Makes employers who underpay workers pay double or triple damages, fines them per employee, and guarantees paystubs and final paychecks.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to strengthen wage-theft penalties was introduced June 24, 2026 with 25 cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents, and has sat in the Senate labor committee with no further action since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a federal right to a paystub showing how pay was calculated, require a final paycheck within 14 days of leaving a job, and make employers who steal wages pay interest plus double or triple damages, with civil fines up to $250,150 per employee for repeat violators. It would extend the deadline to sue from 2 years to 4 (5 for willful violations), stop the clock while the Labor Department investigates, ban forced-arbitration clauses that keep wage claims out of court, and fund grants to community groups that help workers recover unpaid wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers pay less than the minimum wage, skip overtime, require off-the-clock work, misclassify them as contractors, or keep tips — the bill estimates wage theft costs workers over $50 billion a year. Low-wage workers, women, immigrants, and Black workers are disproportionately affected, and they gain the clearest tools: paystubs that reveal violations, longer time to sue, bigger damages, and access to court rather than arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers facing unpaid wages or tips

how_it_helps.text: Employers must give every worker an itemized paystub showing hours, rates, overtime, and deductions, and disclose pay rate and exemption status within 15 days of hire, in the worker's primary language [S2].
Workers fired or quitting must receive all final pay and accrued benefits within 14 days, with the employer owing the worker's regular daily pay for every day of delay up to 30 days [S2].

An employer caught stealing wages owes the unpaid wages, interest, and liquidated damages equal to twice the amount — triple for retaliation — and the court right cannot be waived by a forced-arbitration clause signed at hire [S2].

Civil fines rise to $25,150 per employee per violation, up to $250,150 for repeat or willful violations; willful record falsification plus wage violations must be referred to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution, with criminal fines raised to $100,000 per affected employee [S2].

The window to sue doubles from 2 years to 4 (5 for willful violations) and is suspended while the Labor Department investigates; if an employer kept no records, the worker's own testimony creates a presumption that their account of unpaid hours is accurate [S2].
The Labor Department would fund grants to community organizations, legal aid groups, and unions to educate workers, gather evidence, and help recover back pay, with a GAO study of what works [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who violate wage-and-hour laws, through doubled damages, fines per employee, and possible criminal referral; compliant employers face new costs to produce paystubs, make disclosures, and turn over payroll records on request within 21 days; taxpayers fund the grant program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Underpaying employers and compliant businesses' paperwork

drawbacks.text: Businesses — including small ones — face real administrative costs to produce detailed paystubs, hire-date disclosures, and record inspections for every covered employee [S2].

Doubling or tripling damages and raising fines per employee increases litigation exposure for any employer with a genuine pay-calculation dispute, which supporters of current law argue can punish honest mistakes alongside theft [S2].

The bill overrides arbitration agreements that employees signed voluntarily, which businesses and arbitration providers argue resolves disputes faster and cheaper than court; the bill's answer is that such clauses shield repeat violators from accountability [S2].
The grant program authorizes unlimited appropriations through fiscal 2030 with no stated cap [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the estimated millions of workers shortchanged each year, the bill targets the mechanics that let wage theft persist today: no federal paystub requirement, weak penalties, short filing deadlines, and arbitration clauses that keep claims out of court. The costs fall mainly on violators and on paperwork for compliant firms, though doubled damages and per-employee fines are broad enough to reach honest miscalculations, and the arbitration ban is the most contested piece.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 24, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has remained with no markup, vote, or floor action since.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced S. 4919 on June 24, 2026, joined by 25 cosponsors — 24 of the Senate's 45 Democrats and Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on [S3][S4].

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; the action history shows no further step — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action [S4].
The bill's stated findings estimate wage theft costs workers more than $50 billion per year and that in certain industries compliance with federal wage and hour law is below 50 percent [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers who underpay workers: the current enforcement system, with its two-year filing window, equal-amount damages, and no federal paystub mandate, remains unchanged while the bill sits without action.

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 25 cosponsors

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 24, 2026; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors are Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders — 24 of the Senate's 45 Democrats — and no Republican has signed on, in a chamber where Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats [S3].

industries.industry: Employers with wage-and-hour violations (e.g. fast food, home care, construction, staffing agencies)
industries.note: These employers face unpaid wages plus interest, double or triple damages, fines up to $250,150 per employee, a doubled-to-quadrupled statute of limitations, and mandatory criminal referral for willful falsification. Their cost of keeping stolen wages rises sharply, which is precisely where workers' gains come from.

The bill bars employers from requiring workers to waive their day in court on wage claims as a condition of employment, cutting demand for arbitration of wage disputes. Arbitration of wage claims has been a key reason workers with valid claims often never reach court.

industries.industry: Labor unions, legal aid, and community organizations
industries.note: They become eligible for federal grants to run worker-rights outreach, help file claims, collect evidence, and partner with Wage and Hour Division investigations. The funding supports their existing mission of recovering wages for workers.

They bear new paystub, disclosure, and record-inspection duties, but the bill removes the competitive advantage violators currently gain by underpaying workers. Their interest in a level playing field runs with workers'.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to committee in the final months of a Congress rarely reach the floor, and this one has no Republican cosponsors in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats and control the committee schedule and floor calendar. Unless it picks up Republican support and a committee markup, it will likely die at the end of this Congress in January 2027 without a vote, as similar wage-theft bills in prior Congresses have.
